title: Effect of Deterministic Validation and Single‑Step Repair on Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Outputs: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (Npairs = 1000) that isolates downstream deterministic validation plus at‑most‑one repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. A single sampled initial generation per task (declared model: gpt‑5‑mini; recorded temperature = null/unset) was deterministically reused by two arms: baseline (reuse unchanged) and guarded (validate → possibly invoke one repair → revalidate). Tasks were drawn deterministically from a synthetic NetOps stress corpus and scored by a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Observed paired outcomes: n11 = 995, n10 = 5, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total hosted model calls = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We present the exact McNemar as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, treat the bootstrap CI as a descriptive summary, and label any one‑sided test as exploratory/post‑hoc. We interpret the small absolute guarded gain in the context of sparse discordant counts, near‑unity baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction: Automated intent→configuration translation for network operations can reduce manual effort but introduces safety risks: incorrect sequencing, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference may produce unsafe live changes. Prior literature documents LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that motivate verifier‑augmented pipelines and constrained‑decoding approaches [1],[2]. However, practical evaluations often conflate first‑pass generation interventions (e.g., constrained decoding or prompt engineering) with downstream verification/repair. This study asks a focused question under strict preregistration and shared_initial_candidate semantics: starting from the exact same sampled initial candidate, to what degree can a deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes versus reusing that same candidate without downstream repair (baseline)? The design intentionally holds initial generation constant so any paired outcome difference is attributable solely to deterministic validation and the permitted repair. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic task selection (1000 pairs) and archived validator traces; (2) explicit runtime accounting and model configuration reporting (declared model = gpt‑5‑mini; recorded temperature = null/unset — null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0); and (3) artifact‑grounded interpretation that the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625) while the preregistered paired bootstrap percentile CI is [0.001, 0.01] (descriptive).
sections.related_work: Surveys and controlled studies show LLMs presently suffer from hallucination and prompt sensitivity that reduce the correctness of generated code and configurations, motivating verifier‑augmented designs and constrained output methods [1],[2],[3]. Work on constrained/schema‑aware decoding demonstrates reductions in syntactic and execution errors for structured outputs, though many demonstrations originate outside NetOps and require validator/tool fidelity to transfer [4],[5]. Recent NetOps‑focused system and benchmark papers argue for verifier‑assisted repair, governance, and evidence‑bearing execution protocols; these contributions present prototypes and benchmarks but emphasize dependence on validator coverage and orchestration policies rather than on any single model [6],[7]. Our study complements these works by preregistering a paired comparison that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation and a single limited repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics, thereby avoiding conflation with first‑pass generation interventions.
sections.methodology: Design and preregistration. The full preregistered plan (study_id = cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen before any hosted‑model calls. Key preregistered elements applied here: confirmatory paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks from a synthetic challenging corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both arms); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary prespecified summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) as a descriptive statistic. The execution manifest and analysis artifacts record and reproduce these choices.
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary outcomes. Execution completed per the preregistration: planned episodes = 2000; completed episodes = 2000; complete_pairs = 1000; failed episodes = 0. Provider call audit reports hosted model call event count = 1005 (shared_initial_generation = 1000; repair = 5). The observed paired contingency table is n11 = 995, n10 = 5, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 2). Observed marginal success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test yields p = 0.0625, so the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis is not supported at two‑sided α = 0.05. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01] and is reported as a descriptive secondary summary. An exploratory one‑sided McNemar (not preregistered) gives p = 0.03125 and is explicitly labelled post‑hoc/exploratory.
sections.discussion: Interpretation within preregistered semantics. Under generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate both conditions begin from the identical sampled candidate; only deterministic validator decisions and the permitted single repair call can produce paired differences. Thus the observed five discordant pairs (n10 = 5) directly reflect validator‑triggered corrections where repair succeeded and baseline reused the unsafe candidate. Representative validator traces (archived) indicate initial candidates were rejected for required_sequence violations or protected‑interface touches and accepted after a single permitted repair in the guarded pipeline. Mechanistic reading is therefore: the guarded pipeline can avert specific ordering or protected‑field violations detectable by the validator, but its measurable marginal gain depends on how often such violations appear in the sampled initial candidates and on validator coverage.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment isolating downstream effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) over a baseline that reused the same initial candidate; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls = 1005. These artifact‑grounded results show validator‑guided repair can prevent some unsafe configurations in synthetic NetOps workflows, but detectable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already near‑unity and when the design intentionally isolates downstream interventions. Broader evaluation across different generator semantics (independent first‑pass generations), larger permitted repair budgets, expanded validator rule suites, and multiple model families is needed to map where verifier/repair layers produce operationally meaningful improvements. Our preregistered execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived to enable reproducible follow‑ups and targeted power re‑estimation for settings with higher baseline failure rates.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
